security_audit.summary: All 31 static findings are false positives caused by Markdown formatting, database method names, schema identifiers, and documentation links. Two implementation examples contain real security-relevant weaknesses: disabled transport security and a DynamoDB write path that does not enforce its claimed concurrency condition.

remediation.issue: The EventStoreDB example disables TLS in its connection URI.
remediation.suggestion: Use a TLS-enabled URI by default and label plaintext localhost access as development-only.

remediation.issue: The DynamoDB append example uses batch writes without conditional version enforcement.
remediation.suggestion: Use transactional conditional writes that reject existing stream versions and verify the expected latest version atomically.

semantic_findings.title: Transport Security Disabled in EventStoreDB Example
semantic_findings.description: The example connection URI explicitly disables TLS. Reusing this configuration beyond isolated local development could expose event data and credentials in transit.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The URI explicitly contains tls=false, so transport encryption is disabled. The localhost host reduces immediate exposure but does not make the template safe for deployment.

semantic_findings.title: DynamoDB Example Does Not Enforce Optimistic Concurrency
semantic_findings.description: The append method claims conditional concurrency but uses batch put operations without conditions. Duplicate keys can replace historical events and violate append-only integrity.
semantic_findings.confidence_reasoning: The method derives versions locally and calls batch.put_item without a condition or transaction. DynamoDB put operations replace items with matching keys.

content.value_statement: Event-sourced systems fail when ordering, concurrency, and replay behavior are designed incompletely. This skill provides architecture guidance, technology comparisons, schemas, and implementation patterns.
actual_capabilities: Compares EventStoreDB, PostgreSQL, Kafka, DynamoDB, and Marten for event storage.
Defines append-only storage requirements, ordering models, versions, subscriptions, and idempotency.
Provides a PostgreSQL schema for events, snapshots, indexes, and subscription checkpoints.
Shows Python patterns for appending events, reading streams, and processing subscriptions.
Explains event metadata, snapshot policies, replay safety, and projection rebuilding.
limitations: The examples require adaptation, dependency setup, and testing before production use.
The skill does not benchmark technologies against a specific workload or budget.
The examples do not provide complete authentication, authorization, encryption, monitoring, or disaster recovery.
Technology guidance cannot replace review of current vendor documentation and service constraints.

use_cases.title: Plan a New Event Store
use_cases.description: Compare storage technologies and define ordering, concurrency, subscription, and retention requirements before implementation.

use_cases.title: Implement PostgreSQL Persistence
use_cases.description: Create an event schema and service design for teams that already operate PostgreSQL.

use_cases.title: Review Replay and Scaling Safety
use_cases.description: Assess checkpoints, idempotency, snapshots, projections, and indexes before increasing event volume.

prompt_templates.title: Define Basic Requirements
prompt_templates.prompt: Design an event store for [application]. Ask about event volume, ordering, consistency, retention, replay, and operational constraints before recommending an approach.

prompt_templates.title: Compare Storage Technologies
prompt_templates.prompt: Compare PostgreSQL, EventStoreDB, Kafka, and DynamoDB for [workload]. Evaluate stream reads, global ordering, subscriptions, operations, cost, and scaling.

prompt_templates.title: Design a Production Schema
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a production event-store schema for [domain] using [database]. Include concurrency, idempotency, metadata, indexes, checkpoints, snapshots, retention, and migration strategy.

prompt_templates.title: Audit an Existing Event Store
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this event-store design: [design]. Identify integrity, concurrency, replay, projection, security, recovery, and scaling risks. Prioritize fixes and define verification tests.

output_examples.input: Choose storage for an order service using PostgreSQL with moderate traffic.
output: Recommendation: use PostgreSQL with one ordered stream per order and a global sequence for subscriptions.
Enforce a unique stream and version constraint, then handle conflicts as optimistic concurrency failures.
Store correlation identifiers in metadata and checkpoint each projection independently.

output_examples.input: Review a projection consumer that may receive duplicate events.
output: Primary risk: repeated delivery can apply the same state change more than once.
Record processed event identifiers or make every projection update naturally idempotent.
Advance the checkpoint only after the projection transaction succeeds.

output_examples.input: Plan snapshots for long-lived account streams.
output_examples.output: Create snapshots after a measured event threshold, retain their source version, and verify state by replaying events after that version.

best_practices: State ordering, consistency, replay, retention, and throughput requirements before selecting technology.
Protect event integrity with immutable records, atomic version checks, idempotent writes, and tested recovery procedures.
Validate every example against current libraries, production security controls, and realistic load tests.
anti_patterns: Do not modify or delete historical events to correct domain state.
Do not advance consumer checkpoints before handlers and projection writes succeed.
Do not treat sample connection settings or storage code as production-ready configuration.

faq.question: Does this skill choose a database automatically?
faq.answer: No. It compares common options and uses your workload, operations, consistency, and query requirements to guide selection.

faq.question: Can it design a PostgreSQL event store?
faq.answer: Yes. It covers event tables, stream versions, global positions, snapshots, indexes, and subscription checkpoints.

faq.question: Does it support EventStoreDB and DynamoDB?
faq.answer: Yes. It includes conceptual guidance and Python examples, but those examples require security and production hardening.

faq.question: How does it address concurrent writes?
faq.answer: It recommends expected stream versions and optimistic concurrency. Your implementation must enforce version checks atomically in the chosen database.

faq.question: Does it cover event schema evolution?
faq.answer: It recommends event versioning and explicit upcasting or downcasting policies. It does not provide a complete migration framework.

faq.question: Is the generated design ready for production?
faq.answer: No. Validate authentication, encryption, authorization, observability, recovery, performance, and vendor-specific behavior before deployment.
